name: To the Lighthouse
teaser: Woolf's 1927 novel of the Ramsay family's summers on the Isle of Skye — the trip to the lighthouse postponed, the mother's death, and time passing like weather. The modernist novel at its most luminous.

exploreAction.targetName: The Window section and Time Passes
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening section, where Mrs. Ramsay's dinner holds the family together, then Time Passes. Notice how Woolf renders what is not said. Write what the lighthouse means to each character — and what arriving there at the end completes.

name: Orlando
teaser: Woolf's 1928 fantasy-biography of a poet who lives for centuries and changes sex — a love letter to Vita Sackville-West, and the most playful of Woolf's novels. Time, gender, and glory as a game.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the boy and the centuries
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orlando moves from the Elizabethan court into the centuries. Notice how Woolf treats history as costume and gender as costume. Write what the novel's freedom from biography's rules allows it to say about identity.

name: A Room of One's Own
teaser: Woolf's 1929 essay on women and fiction — the locked library, the imaginary Shakespeare's sister, and the famous claim that a woman needs money and a room of her own to write. The founding text of feminist criticism.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Beadle and the library
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the essay's narrator is turned away from the library and from the grass. Notice how Woolf turns argument into narrative. Write what 'Shakespeare's sister' illustrates about talent and circumstance.

name: A Passage to India
teaser: Forster's 1924 novel of Dr. Aziz, Mrs. Moore, and the Marabar Caves — a friendship across empire tested by accusation and echo. The novel that asked whether connection can survive politics.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mosque and the caves
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Aziz meets Mrs. Moore in the mosque, then read the cave scene. Notice how Forster withholds what happened in the cave. Write what the echo — 'boum' — represents, and why the novel refuses to resolve it.

name: Howards End
teaser: Forster's 1910 novel of the Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and the house that means England — 'Only connect.' The novel of class, culture, and who inherits the land.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the house and the families
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the connection between the cultured Schlegels and the practical Wilcoxes is established. Notice how Forster turns the house into the novel's conscience. Write what 'only connect' asks of people divided by class.

name: Sons and Lovers
teaser: D. H. Lawrence's 1913 novel of Paul Morel, his coal-miner father, and the mother who claims his soul — the Oedipal novel that scandalized and defined modern English fiction. Class, passion, and the family knot.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the mother and the sons
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the marriage of Walter and Gertrude Morel founders and the children become her consolation. Notice how Lawrence renders family feeling with raw intimacy. Write what the novel says about mothers, sons, and the women who come between.

name: Women in Love
teaser: Lawrence's 1920 sequel to Sons and Lovers — two sisters, two men, and the search for a love that is not possession, ending in the Alps. His most philosophical novel, and his most radical.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the wedding and the sisters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Ursula and Gudrun meet Birkin and Gerald. Notice how Lawrence uses the wedding as a stage for his ideas about love and power. Write what the novel proposes love might be, beyond ownership.

name: Lady Chatterley's Lover
teaser: Lawrence's 1928 novel of Constance Chatterley and the gamekeeper Mellors — the most famous banned book of the 20th century, prosecuted for obscenity in 1960, and finally read as the tender novel it is.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the marriage and the estate
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Connie's sterile marriage to the paralyzed Clifford is established. Notice how Lawrence links the body's freedom to the book's politics. Write what the novel's frankness was really arguing against in 1928.

name: The Good Soldier
teaser: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel of two couples and nine years of friendship — 'the saddest story' told by the most unreliable narrator in fiction. Dowell's calm confession hides everything it reveals.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the confession begins
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Dowell announces the tragedy and then circles it. Notice how the narrator's omissions are the plot. Write what the novel's technique — telling everything and understanding nothing — says about marriage and memory.

name: Of Human Bondage
teaser: Maugham's 1915 semi-autobiographical novel of Philip Carey, the clubfoot and the artist's life — love for the impossible Mildred, poverty in Paris, and the slow education of the heart. The bildungsroman to end bildungsromans.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the school and the clubfoot
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Philip's disability and his orphanhood are established. Notice how Maugham narrates suffering with cool clarity. Write what Philip learns through his bondage to Mildred — and what the novel's ending forgives.

name: The Razor's Edge
teaser: Maugham's 1944 novel of Larry Darrell, who returns from the Great War and refuses the American dream to seek enlightenment in India — told by a narrator who is Maugham himself. The spiritual quest novel of its era.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the return and the refusal
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Larry's refusal of a career is met with bafflement. Notice how Maugham frames the quest through the society that cannot understand it. Write what the title's 'razor's edge' — the hard path — means in the novel.

name: Brighton Rock
teaser: Greene's 1938 novel of Pinkie, a teenage gangster in Brighton who believes in hell — and of the girl who knows too much. A thriller that is really a novel about damnation and mercy.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the pier and the killing
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the murder and Pinkie's world are established. Notice how Greene uses the seaside's gaudy surface against the moral darkness. Write what Pinkie's Catholicism — his certainty of damnation — does to his choices.

name: The Quiet American
teaser: Greene's 1955 novel of Saigon in the early Vietnam years — Fowler the jaded journalist, Pyle the idealistic American, and the woman they both love. The novel that warned about American innocence abroad.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the body in the river
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Pyle's death is revealed and then narrated backward. Notice how Greene uses the love triangle to frame the politics. Write what the novel suggests about good intentions — and why it was hated when published.

name: Burmese Days
teaser: Orwell's 1934 first novel of the British Raj in Burma — the timber business, the club, and the one decent man trapped among racists. The novel that taught Orwell what empire was made of.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the club and the district
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the colonial club's petty hierarchies are established. Notice how Orwell exposes the racism that polite fiction of the time ignored. Write how the novel's firsthand anger shaped everything Orwell wrote later.

name: Down and Out in Paris and London
teaser: Orwell's 1933 memoir of poverty — the Paris kitchens, the London doss-houses, and the tramps' code of the road. The book that taught Orwell how the poor actually live, from the inside.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the Paris hotel kitchen
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orwell works as a plongeur in a Paris hotel. Notice how he reports humiliation with dry precision. Write what the book's sociology of poverty — the tramp, the spike, the casual ward — gave to his later politics.

name: Homage to Catalonia
teaser: Orwell's 1938 account of fighting in the Spanish Civil War — the trenches, the lice, and the betrayal of the revolution by its own allies. The book that made him a socialist and a skeptic of all causes.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the militia and the front
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Orwell joins the POUM militia and experiences the war's strange quiet. Notice how he narrates both the idealism and the absurdity. Write what the May Days in Barcelona taught him about power and truth.

name: The Brave Little Tailor and Other Tales
teaser: The Grimms' fairy tales of the tailor who kills seven flies and conquers giants — along with Rapunzel, Rumpelstiltskin, and the stories that shaped childhood for two centuries. The collected dark magic of the European folk tale.

exploreAction.targetName: A selection of tales, including The Brave Little Tailor
exploreAction.instruction: Read several tales, noticing how the Brothers Grimm preserved the stories' violence and wonder. Write what the tales assume about justice, luck, and the world — and why children have always needed their darkness.

name: The Little Prince
teaser: Saint-Exupéry's 1943 novella of a pilot stranded in the desert who meets a prince from a small planet — a fable about grown-ups, roses, and what is essential. The most translated book in the world after the Bible.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the drawing and the meeting
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the narrator's childhood drawing frames the whole book. Notice how the prince's questions expose the absurdity of adult priorities. Write what the book means by 'what is essential is invisible to the eye.'

name: Night
teaser: Elie Wiesel's 1958 memoir of his boyhood in Auschwitz and Buchenwald — the night his faith died with his father, and the silence that followed. The essential testimony of the Holocaust, in a voice that refuses comfort.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Sighet and the arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the community's denial gives way to the cattle cars and the selection. Notice how Wiesel's spare prose carries the enormity without melodrama. Write what the memoir says about the silence of God and the duty of witness.
